## Summary

Research confidence is **Low**. Sources do not yet confirm this break's best wind. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Sources disagree about the best wind direction.
- The sources found do not support this break's listed tide preference.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the wave size this break works in.
- No survey, scientific or official source describes the shape of the bottom.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Ten sources from seven publishers: Surf-Forecast, Wikipedia, Surfertoday (403, kept from the search pass), WannaSurf, Surf Atlas (four pages, one publisher), Stormrider and WSL. Wind dispute: only Surf-Forecast supports the profile's NE (45). WannaSurf gives SE-E (112), Surf Atlas's season guide gives E-SE (112), and Surf Atlas's Morocco page says east (90, the 45-deg edge). The direct evidence leans east, not northeast, so the profile's 45 deserves review. Tide: no source supports the profile's mid. Surf-Forecast says low; WannaSurf and Surfertoday say all tides. On a small WSL contest day in 2023 the waves broke at low tide and stopped as the tide rose (an observation, not recorded as a value). Size: WannaSurf 3 to 16+ ft, Surfertoday 3-15 ft, Surf Atlas up to 10-12 ft and '2-3 m without issue'; the profile's 3-12 ft fits the core, but two sources say it holds more. Swell direction: NW everywhere; WannaSurf adds N and Surf Atlas adds W. Season: November to April (Surf Atlas), September to April for the area (Wikipedia), summer mostly flat (Surf-Forecast); October is the weakest-supported profile month. Period: only qualitative (groundswell, long period); no numbers. Bottom conflict: sand (Surf Atlas Taghazout), sand with rock (WannaSurf), sand and reef (Surfertoday), a rock thumb point (Surf Atlas guide). Ride length conflict: 300-500 m (WannaSurf, Surfertoday), over 1 km (Stormrider), about 2 km linked with Hash Point (Wikipedia). Gaps: no official Moroccan or peer-reviewed source on conditions. Crossref found only Taghazout tourism-geography (Via Tourism Review 2014, read: no spot conditions), seawater-quality and shoreline-change papers.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 3 ft | documented | S3, S4 | `wave_height_min_ft` 3 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | up to 12 ft | documented | S5, S6 | no separate setting; working range 3–12 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 15–16 ft | documented | S3, S4, S9 | `wave_height_max_ft` 12 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: Surfertoday says it starts working at about 3 ft and WannaSurf at 1.0-1.5 m / 3-5 ft (the page's own conversion); neither excerpt says whether this is breaking face height or offshore swell height (WannaSurf labels it 'Swell size'), and Surfertoday was seen only as a search summary.
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “it starts working at about 3 feet and holds up to 15 feet”
  - S4 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”
- **Ideal range**: Surf Atlas says the best swell heights are up to 10-12 ft (no lower bound, and 'swell heights' without saying face or offshore); the same publisher's guide says it takes 2-3 m without issue (2 x 3.28 = 6.6 to 3 x 3.28 = 9.8 ft), which fits inside that.
  - S6 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “Best swell heights are up to 10-12 foot here, which is regular in the winter months.”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “It can take on 2-3 meters without issue”
- **Maximum suitable**: Surfertoday says it holds up to 15 ft and WannaSurf up to 5 m / 16 ft and over (within 25 % of each other, so recorded as agreeing); Stormrider says it can hold huge waves without a number; no excerpt says whether these are face or offshore swell heights.
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “it starts working at about 3 feet and holds up to 15 feet”
  - S4 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”
  - S9 (Stormrider Surf Guides): “Anchors (or Ankas) has the ability to hold huge waves and break down the perfectly angled headland for over a kilometre.”

- **Ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast gives northwest as the best swell direction and Surfertoday says it works best with northwest swells; NW = 315 deg.
  - S1 (Surf-Forecast.com): “the best swell direction is from the northwest”
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “a legendary right-hand point break that works best with long-period northwest swells”
- **Acceptable range**: WannaSurf lists N and NW (315-360) as good directions and Surf Atlas says any good NW-W swell (270-315) works; the value is the span of the two stated windows, which share NW.
  - S4 (WannaSurf): “Good swell directionNorth, NorthWest”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “it's enough to create a point that harnesses any good NW-W swells”

- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it a quite exposed point break with very reliable surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat.
  - S1 (Surf-Forecast.com): “La Point des Ancres in Central Morocco is a quite exposed point break that has very reliable surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat.”

## Conflicting information

- **Wind · offshore**: Surf-Forecast says it works best in offshore winds from the northeast (45 deg), while two Surf Atlas pages name east offshores (90 deg) and east or southeast-leaning offshores (about 112 deg); NE and E-SE are more than 45 deg apart.
- **Tide · preferred stage**: Surf-Forecast says best around low tide, while WannaSurf and Surfertoday (search summary) say all tides; a 2023 WSL contest report started at low tide and ran until the waves stopped breaking, an observation of one day rather than a stated preference.
- **Seasonality · prime months**: Surf Atlas says the point usually gets good around November, peaks in January and tapers off towards May, while Wikipedia says the Taghazout area's waves work best from September to April; both cover November to April and they differ on September-October, and Surf-Forecast adds that summer is mostly flat.
- **Geography · bathymetry**: Surf Atlas's Taghazout page says the bottom is sand, WannaSurf says sandy with rock, Surfertoday (search summary) says sand and reef, and Surf Atlas's spot guide describes the point as a thumb of rock; no survey of the bottom is cited.
